def-cmp-backward-stable.title: Backward stability
def-cmp-backward-stable.html: An algorithm that computes f(d) is backward stable if, for every input d, its computed output f^(d) is the exact result for nearby data: f^(d)=f(d+Δd) with ‖Δd‖≤cu‖d‖, where c is a modest constant depending only on the dimensions of the problem.

def-cmp-numerical-rank.title: Numerical rank
def-cmp-numerical-rank.html: For a tolerance τ>0, the numerical rank of X is rτ=#{i:σi>τ}. The truncated SVD with k terms is Xk=∑i≤kσiuivi⊤.

def-cmp-standard-model.title: Standard model of floating-point arithmetic
def-cmp-standard-model.html: For floating-point numbers x,y and ∘∈{+,−,×,/}, the computed result satisfies fl(x∘y)=(x∘y)(1+δ),|δ|≤u, and fl(x)=x(1+δ) with |δ|≤u, provided no result overflows or underflows.

def-cmp-sweep.title: Sweep
def-cmp-sweep.html: Let A be symmetric with akk≠0. Sweeping A on pivot k produces the symmetric matrix B with bkk=−1akk,bik=bki=aikakk,bij=aij−aikakjakk(i,j≠k).

eq-cmp-cholesky.html: rjj=(ajj−∑k<jrkj2)1/2,rji=1rjj(aji−∑k<jrkjrki),i>j,

eq-cmp-exact-perturbation.html: 𝛃𝛃𝛆b~−β^=X~+(f−Eβ^)+(X~⊤X~)−1E⊤ε^.

eq-cmp-gamma.html: ∏i=1k(1+δi)ρi=1+θk,|θk|≤γk=ku1−ku.

eq-cmp-normwise.html: ‖E‖2≤ϵ‖X‖2,‖f‖≤ϵ‖y‖.

eq-cmp-perturbation.html: 𝛃𝛃‖b~−β^‖‖β^‖≤κϵ1−κϵ(2+η)+κ2ϵ(1−κϵ)2η,

eq-cmp-residual-perturbation.html: 𝛆𝛆‖ε~−ε^‖‖y‖≤ϵ(1+2κ1−κϵ).

eq-cmp-rule.html: relative forward error≲condition number×backward error.

eq-cmp-svd-rss.html: ‖y−Xb‖2=‖U⊤y−U⊤Xb‖2=∑i≤r(ci−σivi⊤b)2+∑i>rci2.

eq-cmp-tsvd-mse.html: 𝛃𝛃E‖bk−β‖2=∑i>k(vi⊤β)2+σ2∑i≤k1σi2.

exm-cmp-centring.title: Centring a column with a large mean
exm-cmp-centring.title_html: Centring a column with a large mean
exm-cmp-centring.html: A sample of 1000 standard normal values is shifted by c=1,10,…,108, and the centred sum of squares is computed by the three algorithms and compared with its exact value (found in rational arithmetic). At c=106, where κx=1.0×106, the relative errors are 8.9×10−5 for the textbook formula, 8.1×10−12 for updating and 2.7×10−17 for two passes. At c=108 the textbook formula has relative error 3.1: not a single correct digit, and possibly a negative “sum of squares”. Updating gives 7.4×10−10 and two passes 2.3×10−17. Figure 10.2.1 shows the three growth rates κ2u, κu and u.

exm-cmp-dc.title: Leaving out the District of Columbia
exm-cmp-dc.title_html: Leaving out the District of Columbia
exm-cmp-dc.html: Refit the state murder-rate regression with all 51 jurisdictions, including the District of Columbia, which Chapter 6 set aside. The residual sum of squares is 142.53 and the PRESS statistic is 230.52. The largest PRESS residual belongs to the District of Columbia. Its ordinary residual is 4.475 and its leverage 0.506, so its prediction error when it is left out is ε^i/(1−hii)=9.066. Its externally studentized residual is 4.28. By @prp-cmp-loo(c), deleting it reduces the residual sum of squares to 101.96, the value found for the 50 states in @exm-cmp-state-cholesky. The script confirms all 51 deletions three ways: by the formulas, by downdating the augmented triangle, and by refitting.

exm-cmp-grunfeld.title: Firm effects in investment data
exm-cmp-grunfeld.html: Grunfeld’s investment data (n=220: 11 US firms over 20 years, public domain in statsmodels) are modelled with an intercept, the firm’s market value and capital stock, and indicators for all 11 firms: p=14 columns of rank 13. Pivoted QR with a tolerance of 10−10 finds rank 13 and leaves out the indicator for General Motors. Three conventions give three different intercepts: −50.67 for the minimum-norm solution (as statsmodels reports), −20.58 for the in-order rule that marks the last indicator as aliased (as R would), and −70.30 for the basic solution from full pivoting. They agree to every printed digit on everything estimable: the coefficient 0.1101 of market value, 0.3100 of capital, the difference −172.20 between the General Motors and US Steel effects, and the residual sum of squares 523719.

exm-cmp-kahan.title: Kahan’s matrix
exm-cmp-kahan.html: Kahan (1966) gave the upper triangular matrix with diagonal 1,s,s2,…,sm−1 and entries −csi−1 above the diagonal in row i, where c2+s2=1. Its columns are already in pivoted order (a tiny perturbation of the column scaling breaks ties in favour of that order), so pivoted QR leaves it unchanged. With m=100 and c=0.2, the smallest diagonal entry is 0.133, yet the smallest singular value is 3.7×10−9. No diagonal entry hints at this (Figure 10.7.1(a)). Such matrices are rare in practice. Chan (1987) gave the first rank-revealing QR algorithm; factorizations whose bounds in both directions are polynomial in p exist (Hong and Pan 1992) and can be computed efficiently (Gu and Eisenstat 1996). Panel (b) shows the typical case: a 50×10 matrix of rank six plus noise of relative size 10−9. The pivoted diagonal drops by eight orders of magnitude exactly where the singular values do.

exm-cmp-kappa-squared.title: The squared condition number is attained
exm-cmp-kappa-squared.title_html: The squared condition number is attained
exm-cmp-kappa-squared.html: Let δ=10−3 and X=(100δ00),y=(0δ1), so that 𝛃β^=(0,1)⊤, 𝛆ε^=(0,0,1)⊤, κ=1000 and η=1. Perturb only the (3,2) entry of X, by ϵ=10−10. This tilts the weak second column towards the residual. Its coefficient becomes (δ2+ϵ)/(δ2+ϵ2), and the relative change in 𝛃β^ is 1.00×10−4, equal to κ2ϵ=1.00×10−4. A perturbation of relative size 10−10 has changed the answer in the fourth digit.

exm-cmp-lauchli.title: A cross-product matrix that rounds to a singular one
exm-cmp-lauchli.title_html: A cross-product matrix that rounds to a singular one
exm-cmp-lauchli.html: Take δ=10−9 and X=(11δ00δ),X⊤X=(1+δ2111+δ2). The columns of X are independent, and κ(X)=2+δ2/δ=1.41×109. But δ2=10−18 is smaller than u, so 1+δ2 rounds to 1 and the computed X⊤X is the singular matrix of ones. The Cholesky factorization of Section 10.2 fails, and no method applied to the computed normal equations can recover the solution. For y=X(1,1)⊤, the exact least squares estimate is (1,1)⊤ with zero residual. QR, which never forms X⊤X, returns it with relative error 3.9×10−16.

exm-cmp-longley.title: Longley’s data, exactly
exm-cmp-longley.html:
Longley (1967) built his macroeconomic data to test regression programs. With an intercept and six regressors, κ(X)=4.86×109 (Section 6.10; the data are described in @exm-rv-longley). The data are published as decimals, so the exact least squares solution can be computed in rational arithmetic. The script does so and counts the correct significant digits of the worst coefficient for each method:

Method Correct digits
Normal equations (Cholesky) 7.2
Householder QR 10.9
SVD 10.8
statsmodels OLS 10.8
Normal equations after scaling the columns to unit length 7.0

The raw κ predicts about 6 digits from QR and none from the normal equations (Section 6.10). Both predictions are far too pessimistic. After scaling the columns to unit length, κ(XD0)=4.33×104. Then κu≈5×10−12 predicts about eleven digits from QR, and κ2u≈2×10−7 about seven from the normal equations. That is what is observed. Scaling the columns explicitly before forming the normal equations changes nothing, as the argument above predicts. Centring as well reduces the condition number to 1.11×102. That is a reparameterization rather than a scaling (@thm-proj-reparam), and what remains is genuine collinearity among the regressors (Chapter 26).

exm-cmp-moving-window.title: Ten-year regressions of consumption
exm-cmp-moving-window.html: Quarterly US real consumption is regressed on an intercept, real disposable income, real investment, population and unemployment (the public-domain macroeconomic series of @exm-mat-macro-svd), in a window of 40 quarters that slides forward one quarter at a time. Each step adds one row and deletes one. Over the 163 steps, whose windows have condition numbers up to 2.9×106, the fit is maintained in two ways. The first applies two Sherman–Morrison updates to (X⊤X)−1. The second updates and then downdates the augmented triangle. After each step both are compared with a fresh QR fit of the window (Figure 10.6.1). Inverse updating reaches a relative error of 6.2×10−7 and ends at 8.4×10−8. Updating the triangle stays below 1.1×10−10 and ends at 3.6×10−11. Both are cheap. Only one keeps QR’s accuracy.

exm-cmp-orthogonality.title: Loss of orthogonality
exm-cmp-orthogonality.html: For 100×12 matrices with prescribed condition numbers from 10 to 1015, Figure 10.3.1 plots ‖Q^⊤Q^−I‖2 for the computed Q^. At κ=108 classical Gram–Schmidt gives 3.5×10−2, and its columns are no longer an orthonormal basis in any useful sense. Modified Gram–Schmidt gives 4.2×10−9, in line with the bound O(κu) of Björck (1967). The Q accumulated from Householder reflections gives 6.3×10−16, orthogonal to working precision whatever the condition number.

exm-cmp-pinv-discontinuity.title: The pseudoinverse jumps
exm-cmp-pinv-discontinuity.html: Let x1=(1,2,3,4)⊤, let d=(1,−1,−1,1)⊤ be orthogonal to it, and let Xt=[x1, x1+td], with y=(1,3,2,5)⊤. For every t≠0 the column space is the same plane span(x1,d), so the fitted values do not depend on t. The coefficients do. At t=10−6 they are −249999 and 250000, because the coefficients must reproduce a fixed multiple of d using the small difference td of the two columns. At t=0 the rank drops to one. The minimum-norm solution jumps to 0.550 for both columns, and the fitted values jump too, because the d-direction has disappeared from the model. Treating singular values below a tolerance as zero makes the two answers agree. Whether it should is a statistical question: is the difference between the columns signal, or recording error?

exm-cmp-state-cholesky.title: Murder rates by the augmented factorization
exm-cmp-state-cholesky.title_html: Murder rates by the augmented factorization
exm-cmp-state-cholesky.html: For the state data of @exm-proj-fwl-crime (n=50, with an intercept and the percentages in poverty, in single-parent households and urban, so p=4), the augmented factorization (@prp-cmp-augmented) gives the coefficients −9.0946, 0.2538, 0.3980 and 0.0046, and the corner entry d=10.0976, so SSE=d2=101.96. The condition number of X is only 509, and the solution agrees with a QR solution to a relative difference of 2×10−14. The largest leverage is 0.260, and log10⁡det(X⊤X)=11.14. The script also checks the standard errors s‖ej⊤R−1‖ against statsmodels.

exm-cmp-state-qr.title: Sequential sums of squares from one factorization
exm-cmp-state-qr.title_html: Sequential sums of squares from one factorization
exm-cmp-state-qr.html: For the state data of @exm-cmp-state-cholesky, Householder QR (@thm-cmp-householder) gives R with diagonal −7.071, 21.511, 21.609 and 113.413. The first entry is −50: the sign convention of @lem-cmp-reflector makes it negative. The squares of the first four entries of Q⊤y are the sequential sums of squares: 1018.81 for the intercept (which is ny¯2), 102.49 for poverty, 80.04 for single-parent households given poverty, and 0.27 for urbanization given the other two. The remaining 46 entries have squared length SSE=101.96. The urbanization variable adds almost nothing once the other two are in the model, which is what its small coefficient in @exm-proj-fwl-crime suggested. The script checks every number against nested fits, and checks the leverages against the squared row lengths of Q1.

exm-cmp-tolerance.title: A nearly aliased column
exm-cmp-tolerance.html: Add to the Grunfeld regressors (intercept, value, capital) a fourth column equal to value plus capital plus noise of relative size 10−9. Its smallest singular value, relative to the largest, is 4.0×10−10. The default tolerance of numpy.linalg.lstsq, max(n,p)ϵM relative to σ1, treats the matrix as having full rank. It returns coefficients as large as 8.1×105, which spend one more degree of freedom to reduce the residual sum of squares from 1768678.4 to 1768252.5, by 0.02 per cent. With the tolerance set to 10−8, the fourth column is treated as aliased, and the largest coefficient is 38.41.

exm-cmp-tsvd.title: Truncating a polynomial design
exm-cmp-tsvd.html: The powers 1,t,…,t7 at 60 equally spaced points in [0,1] form a design with κ(X)=1.1×105 and smallest singular value 9.0×10−5. Take σ=0.1 and a coefficient vector whose components along v1,…,v8 decay (2,−1.5,1,−0.6,0.3,−0.1,0.05,−0.02), as they do for smooth regression functions. By @eq-cmp-tsvd-mse, least squares has mean squared error 1231055. The best truncation keeps 4 components and has mean squared error 0.21, made up of squared bias 0.10 and variance 0.11. A simulation with 4000 replicates agrees with the formula at every k (Figure 10.4.1). The default numerical tolerance treats the design as having full rank, which it does to working precision. The statistical “effective rank” is set by the noise level instead.

exr-cmp-augmented-leverage.title: B1
exr-cmp-augmented-leverage.html: Show that the leverage of row i of the augmented matrix Z=[X,y] is hii+ε^i2/SSE. Deduce the condition under which the augmented triangle can be downdated, and show that it fails only if hii=1 or deleting case i leaves a model that fits the remaining data exactly.

exr-cmp-basic-vs-minnorm.title: B1
exr-cmp-basic-vs-minnorm.html: In the setting of this section, show that the basic solution and the minimum-norm solution have the same fitted values. Show that the minimum-norm solution is orthogonal to N(X), while the basic solution in general is not. For the one-way layout of @exm-proj-ginverse-numeric, which generalized inverse in that example gives the basic solution that drops the intercept?

exr-cmp-cancellation.title: A2
exr-cmp-cancellation.html: For x=10−10, the computer evaluates (1+x)−1. Use the standard model to show that the result is x+δ(1+x) for some |δ|≤u, where the subtraction itself is exact. Estimate the relative error, and check it numerically. Which of the two operations is responsible?

exr-cmp-chol-hand.title: A1
exr-cmp-chol-hand.html: Compute the Cholesky factor of A=(42−22102−226) by @eq-cmp-cholesky, and use it to solve Ab=(2,14,6)⊤ and to find detA.

exr-cmp-chol-simple.title: A2
exr-cmp-chol-simple.html: For simple regression, X=[1,x], find the Cholesky factor (@thm-cmp-cholesky) of X⊤X and of the augmented matrix, and show that it reproduces the slope Sxy/Sxx of @thm-lm-simple-ls. Where does the centring happen?

exr-cmp-consistent-bound.title: B2
exr-cmp-consistent-bound.html: Show that for consistent data (𝛆ε^=0) the bound reduces to 2κϵ/(1−κϵ). Construct a perturbation f of y alone that changes 𝛃β^ by a relative amount κϵ, so that the bound is attained up to a factor of two.

exr-cmp-delete-column.title: B2
exr-cmp-delete-column.html: Let X=Q1R and let X−j be X without column j. Show that X−j=Q1H, where H is R without column j, which is upper Hessenberg in its last p−j columns. Show that p−j rotations of adjacent rows reduce H to (R−j0⊤), and that R−j is the triangle of X−j. How much does the residual sum of squares rise?

exr-cmp-doubles.title: A1
exr-cmp-doubles.html: Show that the doubles in [1,2) are exactly the numbers 1+k2−52, k=0,1,…,252−1. What is the smallest double greater than 1? What is the largest integer N such that every integer from 0 to N is a double?

exr-cmp-fitted-perturbation.title: B1
exr-cmp-fitted-perturbation.html: Deduce from @eq-cmp-residual-perturbation that the fitted values satisfy 𝛃‖X~b~−Xβ^‖≤ϵ(2+2κ/(1−κϵ))‖y‖. Why are fitted values never κ2-sensitive, even though coefficients can be?

exr-cmp-house-hand.title: A1
exr-cmp-house-hand.html: Find the Householder vector and α of @lem-cmp-reflector for x=(3,4)⊤, and verify Hx=αe1. For x=(1,10−9)⊤, compute v1 with both sign choices in double precision, and explain what goes wrong with the unstable one.

exr-cmp-kahan-null.title: C1
exr-cmp-kahan-null.html: For Kahan’s matrix Km(c), find a vector x with ‖x‖=1 and ‖Kmx‖ exponentially small in m when c is fixed. (Solve Kmx=emsm−1 by back substitution and examine the growth of the entries.) Why does column pivoting not detect this?

exr-cmp-kappa-squared-exact.title: A1
exr-cmp-kappa-squared-exact.html: In @exm-cmp-kappa-squared, find b~ exactly and show that the relative change is ϵ(1−ϵ)/(δ2+ϵ2). For which ϵ is it close to κ2ϵ?

exr-cmp-lauchli-family.title: C1
exr-cmp-lauchli-family.html: For 0<δ≤2−27 let Xδ be the matrix of @exm-cmp-lauchli, and let y=Xδ(3,1)⊤ and y′=Xδ(1,3)⊤. Show that the computed cross-product matrices of [Xδ,y] and [Xδ,y′] are identical (and do not depend on δ), although the exact least squares estimates are (3,1)⊤ and (1,3)⊤. Conclude that no algorithm that starts from the computed cross-product matrix can solve these problems. Is anything special about 2−27?

exr-cmp-matvec.title: B2
exr-cmp-matvec.html: Let A be m×n and b∈Rn. Show that the computed product fl(Ab), each entry an inner product, equals (A+ΔA)b with |ΔA|≤γn|A|. Deduce ‖fl(Ab)−Ab‖≤γnn‖A‖2‖b‖.

exr-cmp-mgs-householder.title: C1
exr-cmp-mgs-householder.html: Show that, in exact arithmetic, Householder QR (@thm-cmp-householder) applied to (0p×pX) produces the same R as modified Gram–Schmidt applied to X up to the signs of its rows, and that with the sign convention of @lem-cmp-reflector its reflection vectors are vj=(ejqj)/2. This is the observation of Björck and Paige (1992), who take α=+‖x‖ and so obtain (−ejqj)/2.

exr-cmp-numerical-rank-char.title: B1
exr-cmp-numerical-rank-char.html: Show that if τ is not a singular value of X, then rτ=min{rankB:‖X−B‖2≤τ}, and that the minimum is attained by the truncated SVD Xrτ.

exr-cmp-pivot-hand.title: A1
exr-cmp-pivot-hand.html: Apply column-pivoted QR (@thm-cmp-rank-revealing) by hand to the matrix with columns x1=(1,1,0,0)⊤, x2=(0,0,1,1)⊤ and x3=(1,1,1,1)⊤ (use Gram–Schmidt on the pivoted columns, which gives the same |rij|). Find the pivot order, R, and the rank. Give the basic solution for y=(1,2,3,6)⊤.

exr-cmp-pivoted-cholesky.title: C1
exr-cmp-pivoted-cholesky.html: Let A be nonnegative definite of rank r. Show that the Cholesky recursion with symmetric pivoting, which at step j moves the largest remaining diagonal entry of the current Schur complement to position j, produces a permutation Π and Π⊤AΠ=R⊤R with R=(R11R1200) and R11 an r×r nonsingular upper triangle. (Use @prp-mat-pd-properties(a).) How is this related to the pivoted QR of Section 10.7?

exr-cmp-pooling.title: B2
exr-cmp-pooling.html: Two groups of observations have sizes na,nb, means ma,mb and centred cross-product matrices Ca,Cb. Show that the pooled data have centred cross-product matrix C=Ca+Cb+nanbna+nb(ma−mb)(ma−mb)⊤. Show that @prp-cmp-welford is the special case nb=1, and explain how the formula allows cross-products to be computed in parallel on separate blocks of data.

exr-cmp-press-balanced.title: A1
exr-cmp-press-balanced.html: Show that PRESS=∑iε^i2/(1−hii)2≥SSE. Show that if all leverages equal p/n, then PRESS=SSEn2/(n−p)2. Evaluate this for the state data with n=51 and p=4, and compare with the actual ratio in @exm-cmp-dc.

exr-cmp-r11-bounds.title: B2
exr-cmp-r11-bounds.html: Show that |r11|=maxj‖xj‖, and deduce |r11|≤σ1(X)≤p|r11|. Combine with @thm-cmp-rank-revealing(b) to show that κ(X)≥|r11/rpp|, so that a large ratio of pivots proves ill-conditioning.

exr-cmp-recursive-residuals.title: C1
exr-cmp-recursive-residuals.html: Feed the rows of [X,y] one at a time into the augmented triangle, as in @thm-cmp-givens(c). For k>p, let tk be the entry left in the new row when case k is added. Show that 𝛃tk=±yk−x(k)⊤β^k−1(1+x(k)⊤(Xk−1⊤Xk−1)−1x(k))1/2, where 𝛃β^k−1 and Xk−1 use the first k−1 cases. Show that under the normal linear model the tk are independent N(0,σ2). These are the recursive residuals of Brown, Durbin and Evans (1975), used to test the constancy of a regression over time.

exr-cmp-ridge-svd.title: C1
exr-cmp-ridge-svd.html: Show that the ridge estimate (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y equals ∑iσiσi2+λcivi. Derive its bias and variance in the form of @prp-cmp-tsvd, and show that for every 𝛃β there is a λ>0 (depending on 𝛃β and σ2) for which its mean squared error is below that of least squares.

exr-cmp-rsvd.title: B2
exr-cmp-rsvd.html: Let X=Q1R be a thin QR and R=URΣV⊤ an SVD of the triangle. Show that X=(Q1UR)ΣV⊤ is an SVD of X, and that the minimum-norm least squares solution can be computed from R and Q1⊤y alone. Why is this attractive when n is much larger than p?

exr-cmp-se-from-R.title: B1
exr-cmp-se-from-R.html: Show that the standard error of β^j is s‖ej⊤R−1‖, where s2=SSE/(n−p) (@thm-lm-sigma2). Show that all p standard errors cost p3/3+O(p2) flops, and all n leverages np2+O(np) flops. Why is computing M itself a bad idea?

exr-cmp-sharpness.title: C1
exr-cmp-sharpness.html: Take data with 𝛃β^=vp and 𝛆ε^≠0, and the perturbation 𝛆𝛆E=ϵσ1ε^vp⊤/‖ε^‖, with f=0. Use @eq-cmp-exact-perturbation to show that, to first order in ϵ, 𝛃𝛆b~−β^=ϵσ1‖ε^‖σp−2vp, so that the relative change is ϵκ2η. Compare with the first-order bound ϵ(2κ+κ(κ+1)η).

exr-cmp-summation.title: B1
exr-cmp-summation.html: Show that recursive summation of x1,…,xn returns ∑ixi(1+θi) with |θi|≤γn−1, and that pairwise summation returns such a sum with |θi|≤γ⌈log2⁡n⌉.

exr-cmp-svd-hand.title: A1
exr-cmp-svd-hand.html: Let X=(111100) and y=(1,3,5)⊤. Find the SVD of X, the set of least squares estimates, the minimum-norm estimate and the SSE.

exr-cmp-tsvd-constrained.title: B3
exr-cmp-tsvd-constrained.html: Show that bk minimizes ‖y−Xb‖ over b∈span(v1,…,vk), and that it is the minimum-norm least squares estimate for the matrix Xk. Interpret bk as least squares after deleting the directions in which X is nearly degenerate.

exr-cmp-uncorrelated-residuals.title: B1
exr-cmp-uncorrelated-residuals.html: In the setting of @prp-cmp-qr-quantities, let Q=[Q1,Q2]. Show that under the linear model with 𝛆Cov(ε)=σ2I, the vector c2=Q2⊤y has mean 0 and covariance σ2In−p, and that 𝛆ε^=Q2c2. Under normality, deduce from c2 alone that SSE/σ2∼χ2(n−p) independently of 𝛃β^ (compare @thm-opt-sampling). Is c2 unique?

exr-cmp-wls-condition.title: B2
exr-cmp-wls-condition.html: Weighted least squares with a diagonal weight matrix W of positive weights is ordinary least squares for W1/2X and W1/2y. Show that κ(W1/2X)≤κ(W1/2)κ(X). Give an example with two very different weights in which κ(W1/2X) is large although κ(X) is small, and one in which it is small although κ(W1/2) is large.

lem-cmp-column-subset.title: Singular values of a submatrix
lem-cmp-column-subset.html: If X1 is formed from some of the columns of X, then σi(X1)≤σi(X) for every i up to the number of columns of X1. The same holds for a submatrix formed from some of the rows.

lem-cmp-gamma.html: Let |δi|≤u and ρi∈{1,−1} for i=1,…,k, and suppose ku<1. Then ∏i=1k(1+δi)ρi=1+θk,|θk|≤γk=ku1−ku.{#eq-cmp-gamma}

lem-cmp-reflector.title: Householder vector
lem-cmp-reflector.html: Let x∈Rm, x≠0, let α=−sign(x1)‖x‖ (with sign(0)=1), and let v=x−αe1. Then v≠0, and H=I−2vv⊤/(v⊤v) satisfies Hx=αe1. The first entry v1=x1−α is a sum of two numbers of the same sign, so |v1|=|x1|+‖x‖. Applying H to a vector w as w−2v(v⊤w)/(v⊤v) costs about 4m flops, and H is never formed.

prp-cmp-add-column.title: Adding a column
prp-cmp-add-column.html: Let X=Q1R be a thin QR factorization of a full-column-rank X, and let z∉C(X). Put r=Q1⊤z, w=z−Q1r, ρ=‖w‖ and q=w/ρ. Then [X,z]=[Q1,q](Rr0⊤ρ) is a thin QR factorization. The residual sum of squares falls by (q⊤y)2 when z is added, and the coefficient of z in the enlarged model is q⊤y/ρ=w⊤y/w⊤w.

prp-cmp-augmented.title: The augmented factorization
prp-cmp-augmented.html:
Let X be n×p of full column rank, suppose y∉C(X), and let Z⊤Z=(X⊤XX⊤yy⊤Xy⊤y)=T⊤T,T=(Rz0⊤d), be the Cholesky factorization (@thm-cmp-cholesky) of the cross-product matrix of Z=[X,y]. Then:

  1. R is the Cholesky factor of X⊤X, the least squares estimate solves 𝛃Rβ^=z, and 𝛃d2=SSE=‖y−Xβ^‖2;

  2. for each k≤p, the residual sum of squares of the regression of y on the first k columns of X is d2+∑j>kzj2. The drop in residual sum of squares when column k joins columns 1,…,k−1 is zk2;

  3. det(X⊤X)=∏jrjj2, (X⊤X)−1=R−1R−⊤, and the leverage of row x(i)⊤ is hii=‖R−⊤x(i)‖2.

prp-cmp-gram-rounding.title: Rounding in the cross-product matrix
prp-cmp-gram-rounding.html: Let X be n×p with full column rank and let A^ be X⊤X computed entry by entry as in @prp-cmp-inner-product. Then A^=X⊤X+ΔA with |ΔA|≤γn|X|⊤|X| entrywise, and ‖ΔA‖2≤pγn‖X‖22. In particular A^ is positive definite whenever pγnκ(X)2<1.

prp-cmp-inner-product.title: Rounding error in an inner product
prp-cmp-inner-product.title_html: Rounding error in an inner product
prp-cmp-inner-product.html: Let x,y∈Rn have floating-point entries and nu<1. The inner product computed by recursive summation, s1=fl(x1y1) and sk=fl(sk−1+fl(xkyk)), satisfies sn=∑i=1nxiyi(1+θi),|θi|≤γn. Consequently |sn−x⊤y|≤γn∑i|xiyi|, and sn=(x+Δx)⊤y for a vector Δx with |Δxi|≤γn|xi|.

prp-cmp-loo.title: Deletion formulas
prp-cmp-loo.html:
Let X have full column rank, let hii<1, and let 𝛃β^(i) and SSE(i) denote the least squares estimate and residual sum of squares computed without observation i. Then

  1. 𝛃𝛃β^−β^(i)=(X⊤X)−1x(i)ε^i/(1−hii);

  2. 𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^(i)=ε^i/(1−hii);

  3. SSE(i)=SSE−ε^i2/(1−hii).

prp-cmp-qr-quantities.title: Least squares from QR
prp-cmp-qr-quantities.html:
Let X=Q(R0) with Q orthogonal and rankX=p, and partition c=Q⊤y as (c1⊤,c2⊤)⊤ with c1∈Rp. Then:

  1. 𝛃β^ is the solution of the triangular system Rb=c1, and SSE=‖c2‖2;

  2. Y^=Q(c10) and 𝛆ε^=Q(0c2);

  3. (X⊤X)−1=R−1R−⊤ and hii=‖ei⊤Q1‖2;

  4. ck2 is the drop in residual sum of squares when column k is added to columns 1,…,k−1, the sequential sum of squares of @def-ss-sequential.

prp-cmp-sweep.title: What sweeping computes
prp-cmp-sweep.html: Let S=Z⊤Z be the cross-product matrix of Z=[z1,…,zm]. Let K be a set of column indices such that ZK has full column rank, and let L be the remaining indices. Sweeping S on the pivots in K, one at a time and in any order, meets only positive pivots and produces the matrix W with blocks WKK=−(ZK⊤ZK)−1,WKL=WLK⊤=(ZK⊤ZK)−1ZK⊤ZL,WLL=ZL⊤(I−MK)ZL, where MK is the projection onto C(ZK). Column j∈L of WKL holds the least squares coefficients of zj regressed on ZK, and WLL holds the residual cross-products. With Z=[X,y] and K the columns of X, the last column of W contains 𝛃β^ and, in its corner, the residual sum of squares.

prp-cmp-tsvd.title: Bias and variance of truncated SVD
prp-cmp-tsvd.title_html: Bias and variance of truncated SVD
prp-cmp-tsvd.html:
Suppose rankX=p, 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ2I, and let bk=∑i≤k(ui⊤Y/σi)vi for k≤p. Then 𝛃E(bk)=∑i≤k(vi⊤β)vi,Cov(bk)=σ2∑i≤kvivi⊤σi2, 𝛃𝛃E‖bk−β‖2=∑i>k(vi⊤β)2+σ2∑i≤k1σi2.{#eq-cmp-tsvd-mse}

Hence bk has smaller mean squared error than the least squares estimate bp iff 𝛃∑i>k(vi⊤β)2<σ2∑i>kσi−2.

prp-cmp-van-der-sluis.title: Equilibrating the columns
prp-cmp-van-der-sluis.html: Let X have full column rank and let D0=diag(1/‖x1‖,…,1/‖xp‖). For every nonsingular diagonal D, κ(XD0)≤pκ(XD).

prp-cmp-welford.title: Updating means and centred cross-products
prp-cmp-welford.html: For vectors x1,x2,… in Rq let mk be the mean of the first k and Ck=∑i≤k(xi−mk)(xi−mk)⊤. With dk=xk−mk−1, mk=mk−1+dkk,Ck=Ck−1+k−1kdkdk⊤.

prp-cmp-weyl.title: Singular values are well conditioned
prp-cmp-weyl.html: For any matrices A and E of the same size and every k, |σk(A+E)−σk(A)|≤‖E‖2.

thm-cmp-cholesky.title: Cholesky factorization
thm-cmp-cholesky.html:
Let A be a p×p positive definite matrix.

  1. There is exactly one upper triangular R with positive diagonal entries such that A=R⊤R.

  2. Its rows are given, for j=1,…,p in turn, by rjj=(ajj−∑k<jrkj2)1/2,rji=1rjj(aji−∑k<jrkjrki),i>j,{#eq-cmp-cholesky}

    and every radicand in it is positive.

  3. The computation takes p3/3+O(p2) flops.

  4. If A=X⊤X and X=QR0 is a QR factorization with Q⊤Q=Ip and R0 upper triangular with positive diagonal, then R0=R.

thm-cmp-givens.title: Givens rotations
thm-cmp-givens.html:
1. For (a,b)≠(0,0) let r=(a2+b2)1/2, c=a/r and s=b/r. The rotation G=(cs−sc) is orthogonal and G(a,b)⊤=(r,0)⊤. Embedded in rows i and k of the identity, it changes only rows i and k of a matrix it multiplies, at 6 flops per column.

  2. Zeroing the subdiagonal of X column by column, each entry against the row above it, produces GX=(R0) with G orthogonal. It takes np−p(p+1)/2 rotations and 3np2−p3 flops to leading order.

  3. (Row-wise QR.) Let R be upper triangular and x∈Rp. There are p rotations, the kth acting on row k of R and on the new row, that reduce (Rx⊤) to (R+0⊤) with R+ upper triangular and R+⊤R+=R⊤R+xx⊤. The cost is 3p2 flops. If R and x are augmented by the response, as in @prp-cmp-augmented, the new row ends as (0,…,0,t), and the residual sum of squares increases by t2.

  4. A rotation of rows i and k creates a nonzero in column j only if row i or row k already had one there.

thm-cmp-householder.title: Householder QR
thm-cmp-householder.html:
Let X be n×p with n≥p.

  1. There are reflections H1,…,Hp, with Hj acting only on coordinates j,…,n (or equal to I), such that Hp⋯H1X=(R0) with R upper triangular of size p×p. Thus X=Q(R0) with Q=H1⋯Hp orthogonal, and X=Q1R where Q1 holds the first p columns of Q. If rankX=p, then R is nonsingular, and changing the signs of the rows of R with negative diagonal entries gives the Cholesky factor of X⊤X.

  2. The reduction takes 2np2−2p3/3 flops to leading order. Applying Q⊤ (or Q) to a vector takes 4np−2p2, and forming Q1 explicitly takes another 2np2−2p3/3.

  3. (Backward stability.) In floating-point arithmetic, the computed R^ is the exact triangular factor of X+ΔX, where each column satisfies ‖Δxj‖≤cnpu‖xj‖. The least squares solution b^ computed from R^ and the computed Q⊤y is the exact least squares solution for data (X+ΔX, y+Δy) with perturbations of the same kind, ‖Δy‖≤cnpu‖y‖. Here cnp is a modest multiple of np.

thm-cmp-perturbation.title: Perturbation of least squares
thm-cmp-perturbation.html:
Under @eq-cmp-normwise with κϵ<1, the matrix X~ has full column rank, and 𝛃𝛃‖b~−β^‖‖β^‖≤κϵ1−κϵ(2+η)+κ2ϵ(1−κϵ)2η,{#eq-cmp-perturbation}

𝛆𝛆‖ε~−ε^‖‖y‖≤ϵ(1+2κ1−κϵ).{#eq-cmp-residual-perturbation}

To first order in ϵ, the coefficient bound is ϵ(2κ+κ(κ+1)η).

thm-cmp-rank-revealing.title: Column-pivoted QR
thm-cmp-rank-revealing.html:
Let X be n×p with n≥p, and let XΠ=Q(R0) be computed by Householder QR (@thm-cmp-householder) with column pivoting.

  1. For every k≤j, rkk2≥∑i=kjrij2. In particular |r11|≥|r22|≥⋯≥|rpp|.

  2. For every k<p, σk+1(X)≤‖R22‖2≤p−k|rk+1,k+1|andσmin(R11)≤σk(X).

  3. In exact arithmetic, if rankX=r, then rkk≠0 for k≤r and R22=0 for k=r. The first r columns of XΠ are a basis of C(X), and XΠ=Q(R11R1200) with R11 nonsingular.

  4. The cost is that of the unpivoted factorization, 2np2−2p3/3 flops, plus O(np) for keeping track of the column norms.

thm-cmp-svd-ls.title: Least squares via the SVD
thm-cmp-svd-ls.html:
1. b is a least squares estimate iff vi⊤b=ci/σi for i=1,…,r. The coordinates vi⊤b for i>r are arbitrary, and the set of least squares estimates is X+y+N(X) with N(X)=span(vr+1,…,vp).

  2. X+y=∑i≤r(ci/σi)vi is the unique least squares estimate of smallest Euclidean norm.

  3. Y^=∑i≤rciui and SSE=∑i>rci2=‖y‖2−∑i≤rci2.

  4. If r=p and Cov(Y)=σ2I, the estimate 𝛃β^=X+Y has 𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2∑i≤pσi−2vivi⊤. In particular 𝛃Var(vi⊤β^)=σ2/σi2, and the total variance is 𝛃trCov(β^)=σ2∑iσi−2.

thm-cmp-updating.title: Updating and downdating a triangular factor
thm-cmp-updating.title_html: Updating and downdating a triangular factor
thm-cmp-updating.html:
Let T be an m×m nonsingular upper triangular matrix with T⊤T=A, and let z∈Rm.

  1. (Adding a row.) There are m rotations, the kth acting on row k of T and on an extra row, that turn (Tz⊤) into (T+0⊤), with T+ upper triangular and T+⊤T+=A+zz⊤.

  2. (Deleting a row.) Let a solve T⊤a=z. The matrix A−zz⊤ is positive definite iff ‖a‖<1. In that case put α=(1−‖a‖2)1/2. Choose rotations Gm,…,G1, with Gk acting on coordinates k and m+1, such that G1⋯Gm(a⊤,α)⊤=(0⊤,1)⊤. Then G1⋯Gm(T0⊤)=(T−z⊤) with T− upper triangular and T−⊤T−=A−zz⊤.

  3. Each operation costs O(m2) flops: 3m2 for (a), and 3m2 plus a triangular solve of m2 for (b).
